body.en:
Data integrity means the data in a database is accurate, valid and consistent. Integrity constraints are rules defined on the columns of a table that the DBMS checks automatically on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. A statement that breaks a rule is rejected with an error, so invalid data never enters the table.

Types of integrity constraints

TypePurposeConstraints
Domain integrityEach value is valid for its column (domain)NOT NULL, CHECK (and data type, DEFAULT)
Entity integrityEach row is unique and identifiableUNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY
Referential integrityLinks between tables stay validFOREIGN KEY, REFERENCES, ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL

Column level and table level

  • Column-level constraint: written with the column definition. It applies to that one column. NOT NULL can only be column level.
  • Table-level constraint: written after all columns. It is required when the constraint uses more than one column (composite primary key, multi-column CHECK).
-- column level
col datatype [CONSTRAINT name] type

-- table level (after all columns)
[CONSTRAINT name] type (col1, col2)

Naming constraints

A constraint can be given a name with CONSTRAINT name (e.g. pk_emp, fk_emp_dept, ck_sal). If no name is given, Oracle creates one like SYS_C008401. Named constraints give clear error messages and are easy to drop, disable or enable.

Constraints can be defined in CREATE TABLE or added later with ALTER TABLE.

A NOT NULL constraint ensures that a column cannot contain NULL: a value must be given for it in every row. By default every column allows NULL.

  • It is a domain integrity constraint.
  • It can be defined only at column level.
  • Inserting NULL gives ORA-01400: cannot insert NULL into (...); updating to NULL gives ORA-01407.
  • DESC shows NOT NULL in the Null? column.
  • Add it to an existing column with ALTER TABLE t MODIFY col NOT NULL; (only if the column has no NULLs). Remove it with MODIFY col NULL.
CREATE TABLE customer (
  cid   NUMBER(4),
  cname VARCHAR2(20) NOT NULL,
  city  VARCHAR2(15)
        CONSTRAINT nn_city NOT NULL
);

Use NOT NULL for mandatory data such as name, date of birth or price.

A CHECK constraint defines a condition that each row must satisfy. A value is accepted only if the condition is TRUE (or UNKNOWN because of NULL).

  • It is a domain integrity constraint: it limits the range or list of valid values.
  • It can be column level or table level; a condition on two or more columns must be table level.
  • Violation gives ORA-02290: check constraint (...) violated.
  • A table can have many CHECK constraints; one column can have several.
  • The condition cannot use sub-queries, SYSDATE, USER, ROWNUM, sequences or values from other rows.
age   NUMBER(2)
      CONSTRAINT ck_age
      CHECK (age BETWEEN 15 AND 30),
gender CHAR(1)
      CHECK (gender IN ('M', 'F')),
CONSTRAINT ck_marks
  CHECK (marks >= 0 AND marks <= 100)

Examples: marks between 0 and 100, salary > 0, gender IN ('M', 'F'), city = UPPER(city).

A UNIQUE constraint ensures that no two rows have the same value in the column (or combination of columns).

  • It is an entity integrity constraint.
  • It allows NULL, and many rows can have NULL, because NULL is not equal to anything.
  • A table can have many UNIQUE constraints.
  • Oracle automatically creates a unique index with the same name to enforce it.
  • A duplicate value gives ORA-00001: unique constraint (...) violated.
  • A column set with a UNIQUE constraint can be referenced by a foreign key.
email VARCHAR2(25)
      CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE,
CONSTRAINT uq_phone UNIQUE (phone)

Typical use: alternate keys such as email, mobile number, Aadhaar number or vehicle number.

A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row of a table. PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL.

  • It is an entity integrity constraint: every row has an identity.
  • A table can have only one primary key (ORA-02260 if you try to add a second).
  • Duplicate values give ORA-00001; NULL gives ORA-01400.
  • Oracle automatically creates a unique index for it.
  • A primary key on two or more columns is a composite primary key and must be defined at table level.
  • It is referenced by foreign keys of child tables.
book_id NUMBER(4)
        CONSTRAINT pk_book PRIMARY KEY

-- composite key: table level only
CONSTRAINT pk_enroll
  PRIMARY KEY (roll, cid)

Choose a value that never changes and is short, e.g. roll number, employee number, product code.

A FOREIGN KEY is a column (or set of columns) in one table whose values must match the primary key or unique key of another table (or of the same table). It creates a parent-child relationship and enforces referential integrity.

  • Parent (referenced / master) table: the table containing the primary key, e.g. DEPT.
  • Child (referencing / detail) table: the table containing the foreign key, e.g. EMP.
  • The keyword REFERENCES names the parent table and column. If the column is omitted, the parent's primary key is used.
  • At table level the keywords FOREIGN KEY (col) are written before REFERENCES.
-- column level
deptno NUMBER(2)
       CONSTRAINT fk_emp_dept
       REFERENCES dept (deptno)

-- table level
CONSTRAINT fk_emp_dept
  FOREIGN KEY (deptno)
  REFERENCES dept (deptno)

Rules enforced

  • A child row can only contain a value that exists in the parent, or NULL; otherwise ORA-02291: parent key not found.
  • A parent row that has child rows cannot be deleted (or its key updated): ORA-02292: child record found.
  • The parent table must be created first and cannot be dropped while it is referenced (ORA-02449); use DROP TABLE dept CASCADE CONSTRAINTS.
  • A self-referencing foreign key refers to the same table, e.g. EMP.MGR REFERENCES EMP(EMPNO).

h.en: ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL

body.en:
By default Oracle does not allow a parent row to be deleted while child rows refer to it. A delete rule written with the foreign key changes this behaviour:

RuleWhen a parent row is deleted
(none) / NO ACTIONDelete is rejected with ORA-02292 while child rows exist
ON DELETE CASCADEAll matching child rows are deleted automatically
ON DELETE SET NULLThe foreign key of matching child rows is set to NULL
deptno NUMBER(2)
       REFERENCES dept (deptno)
       ON DELETE CASCADE

deptno NUMBER(2)
       REFERENCES dept (deptno)
       ON DELETE SET NULL
  • Use CASCADE when child rows have no meaning without the parent (order items of an order, marks of a student).
  • Use SET NULL when child rows should be kept (employees of a closed department).
  • The delete rule is shown in the DELETE_RULE column of USER_CONSTRAINTS.
  • Oracle has no ON UPDATE CASCADE; parent keys should not be changed.

h.en: Adding, Dropping, Enabling and Disabling Constraints

body.en:
Constraints can be managed on an existing table with ALTER TABLE.

Adding constraints

ALTER TABLE item
ADD CONSTRAINT pk_item PRIMARY KEY (icode);

ALTER TABLE item
ADD CONSTRAINT ck_rate CHECK (rate > 0);

ALTER TABLE emp
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_dept FOREIGN KEY (deptno)
REFERENCES dept (deptno);

ALTER TABLE item MODIFY iname NOT NULL;

When a constraint is added, Oracle first checks the existing rows. If any row breaks the rule, the constraint is not created, e.g. ORA-02293 (check), ORA-02437 (primary key), ORA-02299 (unique), ORA-02298 (foreign key) or ORA-02296 (NOT NULL).

Dropping, disabling and enabling

ALTER TABLE item DROP CONSTRAINT ck_rate;
ALTER TABLE dept DROP PRIMARY KEY CASCADE;

ALTER TABLE emp DISABLE CONSTRAINT fk_dept;
ALTER TABLE emp ENABLE CONSTRAINT fk_dept;
  • DROP CONSTRAINT removes the rule permanently.
  • A primary/unique key referenced by a foreign key cannot be dropped (ORA-02273) unless CASCADE is used, which also drops the foreign keys.
  • DISABLE turns a constraint off temporarily, e.g. to load large amounts of data quickly. ENABLE turns it on again and checks all rows.
  • Disabling a primary key also drops its index; enabling re-creates it.

Constraint definitions are stored in the data dictionary.

  • USER_CONSTRAINTS: one row per constraint. Important columns: CONSTRAINT_NAME, CONSTRAINT_TYPE, TABLE_NAME, SEARCH_CONDITION, R_CONSTRAINT_NAME, DELETE_RULE, STATUS.
  • USER_CONS_COLUMNS: the columns used in each constraint.
CONSTRAINT_TYPEMeaning
PPrimary key
UUnique key
RReferential (foreign key)
CCheck (NOT NULL is also stored as C)
SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type,
       table_name, status
FROM user_constraints
WHERE table_name = 'EMP';

Practical 11 (re-implementing the Practical 1 tables with constraints) uses all of these: create the parent tables first with primary keys, then the child tables with foreign keys, CHECK and NOT NULL, and then test valid and invalid rows.

A database object is any named structure stored in the database. Besides tables, Oracle provides:

ObjectPurpose
TableBasic unit of storage: rows and columns
ViewLogical (virtual) table based on a query
SynonymAlternative name for an object
SequenceGenerates unique numeric values
IndexImproves the speed of data retrieval

All objects are created with CREATE, changed with ALTER (where allowed) and removed with DROP. Their details are stored in the data dictionary views USER_TABLES, USER_VIEWS, USER_SYNONYMS, USER_SEQUENCES, USER_INDEXES and USER_OBJECTS.

A view is a virtual table based on the result of a SELECT statement. It has rows and columns like a table but stores no data of its own; only its query is stored in the data dictionary. Each time the view is used, Oracle runs the query on the base table(s), so the view always shows current data.

CREATE [OR REPLACE] [FORCE] VIEW name
  [(alias1, alias2, ...)]
AS SELECT ...
[WITH CHECK OPTION]
[WITH READ ONLY];
  • OR REPLACE: re-creates the view if it already exists.
  • FORCE: creates the view even if the base table does not exist yet.
  • Aliases: column names for the view.
  • WITH CHECK OPTION / WITH READ ONLY: restrict DML through the view.
CREATE VIEW emp20 AS
SELECT empno, ename, job, sal
FROM emp
WHERE deptno = 20;

SELECT * FROM emp20;

Advantages of views

  • Security: users see only selected columns and rows (e.g. no salary).
  • Simplicity: a complex join or calculation is written once and used like a table.
  • Data independence: applications use the view even if the base table structure changes.
  • Different views of the same data for different users.
  • No extra storage is needed.

Disadvantages: a view on a complex query can be slow, and DML through complex views is restricted.

h.en: Simple and Complex Views; DML through Views

body.en:
Simple viewComplex view
Based on one tableBased on one or more tables (joins)
No functions, GROUP BY or DISTINCTCan contain group functions, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, expressions
INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE allowed (usually)DML not always allowed
CREATE VIEW dept_summary AS
SELECT d.dname, COUNT(e.empno) total,
       SUM(e.sal) total_sal
FROM dept d JOIN emp e
ON d.deptno = e.deptno
GROUP BY d.dname;

Rules for DML through a view

  • INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on a simple view change the base table.
  • DML is not allowed if the view contains group functions, GROUP BY, DISTINCT or ROWNUM: ORA-01732.
  • A column defined by an expression (e.g. sal * 12) cannot be inserted or updated: ORA-01733.
  • INSERT through a view fails if a NOT NULL column of the base table is not in the view.
  • For a join view, only the key-preserved table can be modified.

h.en: WITH CHECK OPTION and WITH READ ONLY

body.en:
WITH CHECK OPTION ensures that every row inserted or updated through the view satisfies the view's WHERE condition, so it remains visible through the view. Otherwise Oracle gives ORA-01402: view WITH CHECK OPTION where-clause violation.

WITH READ ONLY prevents all DML operations through the view (ORA-42399). The view can only be queried.

CREATE VIEW emp30 AS
SELECT empno, ename, sal, deptno
FROM emp WHERE deptno = 30
WITH CHECK OPTION;

CREATE VIEW emp_public AS
SELECT empno, ename, job FROM emp
WITH READ ONLY;
  • Through EMP30 you cannot insert an employee of department 10 or move an employee to department 20.
  • Through EMP_PUBLIC users can see employee names and jobs but cannot change anything.
  • A name can be given: WITH CHECK OPTION CONSTRAINT ck_emp30.

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_emp AS
SELECT empno, ename, sal FROM emp;

ALTER VIEW v_emp COMPILE;

DROP VIEW v_emp;
  • CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW is the way to change a view's query. The view keeps its name and the privileges granted on it.
  • ALTER VIEW view_name COMPILE recompiles a view that became invalid after a change to its base table. ALTER VIEW cannot change the query.
  • DROP VIEW removes the view definition only; the base table data is not affected. Views built on the dropped view become invalid.
  • If the base table is dropped, the view becomes invalid and gives an error when used.
  • View definitions can be seen in USER_VIEWS (VIEW_NAME, TEXT).

h.en: Synonyms: CREATE SYNONYM and DROP SYNONYM

body.en:
A synonym is an alternative name (alias) for a table, view, sequence, procedure or another synonym. It stores no data; it only points to the object.

CREATE [PUBLIC] SYNONYM syn_name
FOR [schema.]object_name;

DROP [PUBLIC] SYNONYM syn_name;

CREATE SYNONYM e FOR emp;
SELECT * FROM e;

Types

  • Private synonym (default): owned by a user and usable by that user (and others with privileges).
  • Public synonym: created with PUBLIC by the DBA and usable by all users, e.g. CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM emp FOR scott.emp.

Uses / advantages

  • Gives a short, simple name for a long object name such as scott.employee_details.
  • Hides the owner and real name of the object (location transparency and security).
  • If the object moves, only the synonym is changed; programs stay the same.

SELECT and DML on a synonym work on the real object. DROP SYNONYM removes only the alias. Synonyms are listed in USER_SYNONYMS.

h.en: Sequences: CREATE SEQUENCE, NEXTVAL and CURRVAL

body.en:
A sequence is a database object that generates a series of unique integers automatically. It is mainly used to generate primary key values such as roll numbers, bill numbers or order numbers.

CREATE SEQUENCE seq_name
  [START WITH n]
  [INCREMENT BY n]
  [MINVALUE n | NOMINVALUE]
  [MAXVALUE n | NOMAXVALUE]
  [CYCLE | NOCYCLE]
  [CACHE n | NOCACHE];
OptionMeaning (default)
START WITHFirst number (1)
INCREMENT BYGap between numbers; negative for descending (1)
MINVALUE / MAXVALUELowest and highest value
CYCLE / NOCYCLERestart after MAXVALUE or stop with an error (NOCYCLE)
CACHE n / NOCACHEPre-allocate n numbers in memory for speed (CACHE 20)

Pseudo columns

  • seq.NEXTVAL: returns the next number and advances the sequence.
  • seq.CURRVAL: returns the current (last generated) number in this session; it can be used only after NEXTVAL (else ORA-08002).
CREATE SEQUENCE seq_bill
START WITH 1001 INCREMENT BY 1;

INSERT INTO bill
VALUES (seq_bill.NEXTVAL, 'Aarav');

SELECT seq_bill.CURRVAL FROM dual;

A sequence is independent of tables: one sequence can be used for many tables. Numbers are not rolled back, so gaps can appear after ROLLBACK or a crash.

ALTER SEQUENCE seq_bill
  INCREMENT BY 10
  MAXVALUE 99999
  CYCLE;

DROP SEQUENCE seq_bill;
  • ALTER SEQUENCE can change INCREMENT BY, MINVALUE, MAXVALUE, CYCLE and CACHE. The change affects only future numbers.
  • START WITH cannot be altered (ORA-02283); drop and re-create the sequence to restart it.
  • MAXVALUE cannot be set lower than the current value.
  • With NOCYCLE, NEXTVAL after MAXVALUE gives ORA-08004.
  • DROP SEQUENCE removes the sequence; values already stored in tables stay.
  • USER_SEQUENCES shows SEQUENCE_NAME, MIN_VALUE, MAX_VALUE, INCREMENT_BY, CYCLE_FLAG, CACHE_SIZE and LAST_NUMBER.

h.en: Indexes: Concept, Unique and Composite Index

body.en:
An index is a database object that speeds up the retrieval of rows, just like the index at the back of a book. It stores the column values in sorted order together with the ROWID (address) of each row. Oracle uses an index automatically when a query searches on the indexed column; without an index, Oracle reads every row (full table scan).

CREATE [UNIQUE] INDEX index_name
ON table_name (col1 [, col2 ...]);

DROP INDEX index_name;

Types of indexes

  • Simple (single-column) index: on one column.
  • Composite (concatenated) index: on two or more columns, e.g. (deptno, job). It is used when the WHERE clause uses the leading column(s).
  • Unique index: does not allow duplicate values. Oracle creates one automatically for every PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraint.
  • Non-unique index: allows duplicates (the default).
CREATE INDEX idx_ename ON emp (ename);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_dname
ON dept (dname);

CREATE INDEX idx_dept_job
ON emp (deptno, job);

When to create an index

  • The column is used often in WHERE, JOIN or ORDER BY.
  • The table is large and queries return a small part of its rows.
  • The column has many different values.

When not to

  • Small tables, or columns that are rarely searched.
  • Tables that are updated very often: every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update the indexes, and indexes take disk space.

DROP INDEX index_name; removes an index. The table and its data are not affected; queries still work but may be slower.

  • A unique index cannot be created on a column that already contains duplicates: ORA-01452.
  • The same column list cannot be indexed twice: ORA-01408 (e.g. a primary key column is already indexed).
  • An index used by a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint cannot be dropped directly (ORA-02429); drop or disable the constraint.
  • When a table is dropped, all its indexes are dropped automatically.
  • Indexes are listed in USER_INDEXES and their columns in USER_IND_COLUMNS.
  • Practical 13 also compares query time with and without an index: in SQL*Plus, SET TIMING ON shows the time taken by each statement, and the difference appears clearly on a large table.

• NOT NULL means the column must always have a value. It can only be defined at column level.
  • CNAME has an unnamed NOT NULL (Oracle gives it a SYS_C name); CITY has a named constraint nn_city.

CREATE TABLE student4 (
  roll   NUMBER(3),
  name   VARCHAR2(15),
  gender CHAR(1)
         CHECK (gender IN ('M', 'F')),
  age    NUMBER(2)
         CONSTRAINT ck_age
         CHECK (age BETWEEN 15 AND 30),
  min_m  NUMBER(3),
  marks  NUMBER(3),
  CONSTRAINT ck_marks
    CHECK (marks >= 0 AND marks <= 100)
);

INSERT INTO student4
VALUES (1, 'Aarav', 'M', 18, 35, 82);

VALUES (2, 'Diya', 'X', 17, 35, 91);

VALUES (3, 'Karan', 'M', 12, 35, 67);

VALUES (4, 'Isha', 'F', 19, 35, 120);

title.en: View constraints in the data dictionary

code.en:
SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type,
       table_name, r_constraint_name
FROM user_constraints
WHERE table_name IN ('DEPT', 'EMP')
ORDER BY table_name, constraint_name;

SELECT constraint_name, column_name,
       position
FROM user_cons_columns
WHERE table_name = 'EMP'
ORDER BY constraint_name;

  • REFERENCES branch without a column refers to the parent's primary key.
  • Branch 'ME' does not exist (ORA-02291) and semester 9 is out of range (ORA-02290), so those rows are rejected.
  • The last query counts the constraints of each type in each table (C includes the NOT NULL constraints).

expl.en:
• A view is a stored SELECT statement that behaves like a virtual table. No data is copied; each query on EMP20 reads EMP.
  • The view hides the other columns (MGR, COMM, DEPTNO...) and other departments' rows: a simple way of giving security.
  • A view can be queried, filtered and described just like a table.

expl.en:
• DML on a simple view (one table, no group functions, DISTINCT or expressions) changes the base table.
  • RAVI was inserted into EMP and then deleted; KIRAN's salary in EMP became 24000.
  • Columns not in the view (JOB, MGR ...) are set to NULL or their default when a row is inserted through the view, so NOT NULL columns of the base table must be included in the view.

expl.en:
• A complex view uses joins, group functions, GROUP BY, DISTINCT or expressions. It is very useful for reports.
  • DML on a group view is not allowed: ORA-01732.
  • A column made from an expression (sal * 12) is a virtual column; it cannot be updated (ORA-01733), but the other columns of that view can be.
  • Column aliases can be given in the view header: emp_annual (id, name, annual).

expl.en:
• CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW changes the definition of an existing view without dropping it (privileges granted on it are kept).
  • ALTER VIEW ... COMPILE recompiles a view, e.g. after its base table was changed. (ALTER VIEW cannot change the query.)
  • USER_VIEWS stores the view's query text.
  • DROP VIEW removes only the definition; the data in EMP is not affected. Afterwards the view no longer exists (ORA-00942).

expl.en:
• A synonym is an alias (another name) for a table, view, sequence or other object. It stores no data.
  • All SELECT and DML statements on the synonym work on the real table EMP.
  • It hides the real owner and name, and gives a short name for a long one (e.g. CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM emp FOR scott.emp, so other users need not write scott.emp).
  • After DROP SYNONYM the name no longer exists, but the table is unaffected.

q.en: What is an integrity constraint?

a.en: A rule defined on a table column that the DBMS checks automatically to keep the data valid and consistent.

q.en: Name the three types of integrity constraints.

a.en: Domain integrity (NOT NULL, CHECK), entity integrity (UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY) and referential integrity (FOREIGN KEY).

q.en: What is the difference between column-level and table-level constraints?

a.en: A column-level constraint is written with the column and applies to it; a table-level constraint is written after all columns and can use several columns.

q.en: Which constraint can only be defined at column level?

a.en: NOT NULL.

q.en: When must a constraint be defined at table level?

a.en: When it uses more than one column, e.g. a composite primary key.

q.en: What name does Oracle give to an unnamed constraint?

a.en: A system name like SYS_C008401.

q.en: What does a CHECK constraint do?

a.en: It allows only values for which a given condition is true, e.g. CHECK (marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100).

q.en: Can a UNIQUE column contain NULL?

a.en: Yes, and several rows can contain NULL.

q.en: What is the difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

a.en: A primary key does not allow NULL and there can be only one per table; UNIQUE allows NULLs and there can be many.

q.en: What is a composite primary key?

a.en: A primary key made of two or more columns, defined at table level, e.g. PRIMARY KEY (roll, cid).

q.en: What is a foreign key?

a.en: A column whose values must match the primary or unique key of another (parent) table, or be NULL.

q.en: Which table must be created first: parent or child?

a.en: The parent (referenced) table.

q.en: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?

a.en: When a parent row is deleted, all its child rows are deleted automatically.

q.en: What does ON DELETE SET NULL do?

a.en: When a parent row is deleted, the foreign key in its child rows is set to NULL.

q.en: What is a self-referencing foreign key?

a.en: A foreign key that refers to the primary key of the same table, e.g. EMP.MGR → EMP.EMPNO.

q.en: What is ORA-02291?

a.en: Integrity constraint violated – parent key not found (child value has no matching parent).

q.en: What is ORA-02292?

a.en: Integrity constraint violated – child record found (parent row has children).

q.en: How do you add a primary key to an existing table?

a.en: ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT pk_t PRIMARY KEY (col);

q.en: Why disable a constraint?

a.en: To load or change a large amount of data quickly; it is enabled again afterwards.

q.en: Which dictionary view shows constraints?

a.en: USER_CONSTRAINTS (and USER_CONS_COLUMNS for their columns).

q.en: What is a view?

a.en: A virtual table based on a stored SELECT query; it stores no data.

q.en: Give two advantages of views.

a.en: Security (hide columns and rows) and simplicity (hide complex joins).

q.en: What is the difference between a simple and a complex view?

a.en: A simple view uses one table without functions or grouping and allows DML; a complex view uses joins, functions or GROUP BY and may not allow DML.

q.en: Can we insert data through a view?

a.en: Yes, through a simple view; the row is inserted into the base table.

q.en: What is WITH CHECK OPTION?

a.en: It allows only inserts and updates that produce rows visible through the view.

q.en: What is WITH READ ONLY?

a.en: It prevents any INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE through the view.

q.en: How do you change the query of a view?

a.en: With CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW.

q.en: What happens to the table when a view is dropped?

a.en: Nothing; only the view definition is removed.

q.en: What is a synonym?

a.en: An alternative name (alias) for a database object such as a table or view.

q.en: What is a public synonym?

a.en: A synonym available to all users, created with CREATE PUBLIC SYNONYM.

q.en: What is a sequence?

a.en: A database object that generates unique numbers automatically, mainly for primary keys.

q.en: What is the difference between NEXTVAL and CURRVAL?

a.en: NEXTVAL gives the next number and advances the sequence; CURRVAL gives the last number generated in the session.

q.en: Can CURRVAL be used before NEXTVAL?

a.en: No, it gives ORA-08002.

q.en: What does CYCLE mean in a sequence?

a.en: After reaching MAXVALUE the sequence starts again from MINVALUE.

q.en: Which sequence option cannot be altered?

a.en: START WITH.

q.en: What is the use of CACHE in a sequence?

a.en: Oracle pre-allocates numbers in memory for faster access (default 20).

q.en: What is an index?

a.en: An object that stores sorted column values with ROWIDs to speed up searching.

q.en: What is a composite index?

a.en: An index on two or more columns.

q.en: What is a unique index?

a.en: An index that does not allow duplicate values; created automatically for PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE.

q.en: What is a disadvantage of too many indexes?

a.en: They slow down INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE and use extra storage.

q.en: Does DROP INDEX delete table data?

a.en: No, only the index is removed.
